chemistrykit.AdsorptionIsotherm: BETIsotherm generalizes Langmuir to multilayer adsorption. As the saturation vapor pressure P_0 \to \infty at fixed K=C/P_0, multilayer condensation is suppressed and BET reduces exactly to the Langmuir isotherm -- a reduction verified here numerically, not just asserted.

Paul Sabatier's qualitative principle -- that the best catalyst binds a reaction intermediate neither too weakly (nothing sticks long enough to react) nor too strongly (the surface clogs with product and never frees up for another turnover) -- is illustrated here with the standard modern textbook toy model (see, e.g., Chorkendorff & Niemantsverdriet, Concepts of Modern Catalysis and Kinetics, 2nd ed., Wiley-VCH, 2007, Ch. 8): a two-step surface mechanism whose overall rate needs both an occupied site (to hold the adsorbed intermediate) and an empty site (for the next step to proceed), so the rate is proportional to \theta(1-\theta), with \theta the Langmuir coverage (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.langmuir.langmuir_coverage) set by the adsorption equilibrium constant K -- a proxy for binding strength. This is not a literal reproduction of Sabatier's own (qualitative) or Balandin's (multiplet-theory) equations, just the simplest possible model with the same volcano-shaped structure they established conceptually and structurally, respectively.
The Sabatier principle and the catalytic volcano curve

FreundlichIsotherm models the empirical power law q=K_fP^{1/n}, useful for a heterogeneous surface where Langmuir's single-site-energy assumption breaks down. Unlike Langmuir, it has no saturation limit, so extrapolating it far beyond the fitted pressure range is unphysical. fit_freundlich recovers (Kf, n) via the standard log q vs. log P linearization.

LangmuirIsotherm models monolayer adsorption on a fixed pool of identical surface sites. Its fractional coverage \theta=KP/(1+KP) reaches exactly one-half at the half-saturation pressure P=1/K, and fit_langmuir recovers (K, qmax) from noisy loading-vs-pressure data via the standard 1/q-vs-1/P linearization.

chemistrykit.Brusselator: Below the Hopf-bifurcation threshold (:math:`B < 1 + A^2`) the Brusselator's single fixed point is a stable focus and any initial concentration relaxes toward it. chemistrykit.Buckingham: The Buckingham (exp-6) potential replaces the Lennard-Jones r^{-12} repulsive wall with an exponential -- closer to the true quantum-mechanical electron-overlap repulsion -- while keeping the same r^{-6} dispersion attraction. Matched to a Lennard-Jones potential's well depth, position, and long-range tail, the two agree closely everywhere near and beyond the minimum. But the exponential repulsion is eventually overwhelmed by the unbounded -C/r^6 attractive term at short enough range, so the Buckingham potential has a second, spurious turnover well inside the true minimum: past that point it falls back toward -\infty as r\to0 instead of diverging to +\infty the way Lennard-Jones's pure r^{-12} repulsion does.
Buckingham vs. Lennard-Jones: exponential repulsion and its inner turnover

chemistrykit.EigenstateResult: H2PlusVariational builds the 2x2 Hamiltonian and overlap matrices for a minimal one-Gaussian- per-proton basis, solves the secular equation HC=SCE, and then variationally optimizes the shared Gaussian exponent -- a genuine application of the Rayleigh-Ritz variational theorem: minimizing over a real parameter can only lower (never raise) the computed energy toward the true ground state.

Walter Heitler and Fritz London's 1927 quantum-mechanical treatment of H2 -- the paper usually credited with founding quantum chemistry as a field -- showed for the first time why two hydrogen atoms bind: the symmetric (in-phase) combination of their two atomic orbitals builds up electron density in the region between the nuclei, lowering the energy below that of the separated atoms, while the antisymmetric (out-of-phase) combination depletes density there and raises the energy instead. Their original calculation used two-electron integrals this package does not implement (chemistrykit.quantum.utils.basis_sets stops at the one-electron integrals H2PlusVariational needs for H2+), but the same qualitative physics -- constructive vs. destructive interference of atomic orbitals along the bond axis -- is exactly what H2+'s own bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals show, using the genuine LCAO coefficients solve computes, not an assumed equal-weight combination.
Heitler-London's insight: bonding vs. antibonding electron density

Builds the Huckel secular matrix for butadiene and benzene (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.HuckelSystem), diagonalizes it via numpy.linalg.eigh (a genuine eigenvalue problem, not a lookup table), cross-checks the result against the closed-form Coulson/Frost eigenvalue formulas, and checks Huckel's 4n+2 rule (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.is_aromatic_by_huckel_rule) against the computed spectrum's degeneracies.
Huckel theory: butadiene, benzene, and the 4n+2 aromaticity rule

Two independent routes to a (generally non-integer) bond order: Pauling's empirical bond-length correlation applied to benzene's intermediate C-C bond length, and the Coulson bond order computed directly from Huckel molecular-orbital coefficients for the same molecule -- the two independent methods agree that benzene's C-C bond order sits between 1 and 2.
Bond order: the Pauling length correlation, and the Huckel Coulson bond order

Walter Heitler and Fritz London's 1927 quantum-mechanical treatment of H2 -- the paper usually credited with founding quantum chemistry as a field -- showed for the first time why two hydrogen atoms bind: the symmetric (in-phase) combination of their two atomic orbitals builds up electron density in the region between the nuclei, lowering the energy below that of the separated atoms, while the antisymmetric (out-of-phase) combination depletes density there and raises the energy instead. Their original calculation used two-electron integrals this package does not implement (chemistrykit.quantum.utils.basis_sets stops at the one-electron integrals H2PlusVariational needs for H2+), but the same qualitative physics -- constructive vs. destructive interference of atomic orbitals along the bond axis -- is exactly what H2+'s own bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals show, using the genuine LCAO coefficients solve computes, not an assumed equal-weight combination.
Heitler-London's insight: bonding vs. antibonding electron density
chemistrykit.H2PlusVariational.total_ene: H2PlusVariational builds the 2x2 Hamiltonian and overlap matrices for a minimal one-Gaussian- per-proton basis, solves the secular equation HC=SCE, and then variationally optimizes the shared Gaussian exponent -- a genuine application of the Rayleigh-Ritz variational theorem: minimizing over a real parameter can only lower (never raise) the computed energy toward the true ground state.
H2+ in a minimal 2-Gaussian basis: the variational principle at work
chemistrykit.HalfReaction: faradays_law_mass gives the mass of a species deposited or consumed by a constant current over time. This example verifies the linear proportionality to both current and time (Faraday's first law), computes the minimum applied voltage needed to force a non-spontaneous (electrolytic) reaction to run, and contrasts a spontaneous galvanic reaction against one that needs external electrolysis.
Faraday's laws of electrolysis, and galvanic vs. electrolytic cells

Days after learning of Volta's newly announced pile, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle connected one to a bowl of water in May 1800 and watched gas bubble from each wire -- the first electrolysis, and the first new discovery the pile made possible. This example reconstructs both halves of that observation from functions already in this package: the theoretical minimum decomposition voltage of water (~chemistrykit.electrochem.systems.electrolysis.minimum_applied_voltage_electrolytic, applied to the tabulated H+/H2 and O2/H2O standard potentials) comes out at the textbook 1.23 V, and Faraday's law (~chemistrykit.electrochem.systems.electrolysis.moles_from_charge) recovers the 2:1 hydrogen-to-oxygen ratio Nicholson and Carlisle actually saw bubbling from the two wires, directly from electron-transfer stoichiometry.
Nicholson and Carlisle's electrolysis of water

STANDARD_REDUCTION_POTENTIALS is a small curated table of standard reduction potentials. cell_potential combines any two half-reactions into a standard cell potential, and balance_redox_reaction finds the electron-balancing multiples needed to write out the full mass-balanced overall reaction.
Standard reduction potentials, redox-couple balancing, and cell potentials
chemistrykit.HarmonicBond: The harmonic bond potential (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) is the small-oscillation limit of the anharmonic Morse potential -- they agree near the equilibrium separation but diverge away from it (Morse correctly flattens out toward a finite dissociation energy; harmonic does not). DiatomicOscillator integrates the classical two-body bond-vibration problem via the shared velocity-Verlet integrator, for either potential.

chemistrykit.HarmonicMolecule: HarmonicMolecule builds a small molecular-mechanics "force field" out of nothing but harmonic bond (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) and harmonic angle-bend (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicAngle) terms -- the classical, spring-and-hinge picture of molecular structure that founded molecular mechanics. A bent, water-like triatomic (one heavy vertex atom, two light outer atoms, equilibrium angle 104.5 degrees) is displaced away from its equilibrium geometry and left to vibrate under velocity-Verlet integration alone (no thermostat): both bond lengths and the bond angle oscillate indefinitely about their equilibrium values, and the total energy is conserved to within integration error.
A bent triatomic molecule: coupled bond-stretch and angle-bend vibrations

chemistrykit.HuckelSystem: Builds the Huckel secular matrix for butadiene and benzene (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.HuckelSystem), diagonalizes it via numpy.linalg.eigh (a genuine eigenvalue problem, not a lookup table), cross-checks the result against the closed-form Coulson/Frost eigenvalue formulas, and checks Huckel's 4n+2 rule (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.is_aromatic_by_huckel_rule) against the computed spectrum's degeneracies.

Two independent routes to a (generally non-integer) bond order: Pauling's empirical bond-length correlation applied to benzene's intermediate C-C bond length, and the Coulson bond order computed directly from Huckel molecular-orbital coefficients for the same molecule -- the two independent methods agree that benzene's C-C bond order sits between 1 and 2.

chemistrykit.IdealGas: Comparing three equations of state for carbon dioxide at a fixed temperature: the ideal gas law (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.equations_of_state.IdealGas), van der Waals (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.equations_of_state.VanDerWaals), and Redlich-Kwong (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.equations_of_state.RedlichKwong). chemistrykit.IdealGasMolecule: James Clerk Maxwell (1860) and, in fully general form, Ludwig Boltzmann (1871) showed that every classical quadratic degree of freedom of a system in thermal equilibrium contributes exactly \frac12k_B to its heat capacity -- the equipartition theorem. A rigid diatomic molecule therefore "should" carry \frac32k_B (translation) + k_B (2 rotational degrees of freedom) + k_B (1 vibrational mode, kinetic + potential) = \frac72k_B at every temperature -- a prediction 19th-century equipartition theory could not explain deviations from (Maxwell himself flagged the puzzle sharply in 1879). Only VibrationalPartitionFunctionHarmonic is an exact quantum treatment in this package, so it alone shows the real resolution Einstein gave in 1907: a mode's contribution only "switches on" once k_BT exceeds its own quantum spacing. RotationalPartitionFunctionLinear, by contrast, implements only the classical high-temperature limit (as its own docstring flags), so it contributes its full k_B at every temperature here -- a deliberate approximation, harmless in practice because real rotational spacings are tiny compared to vibrational ones (as the numbers below confirm), but worth seeing explicitly rather than assuming.
The equipartition theorem, and why only one mode actually "freezes out"

chemistrykit.KineticsResult: StoichiometricNetwork integrates an arbitrary mass-action reaction network numerically via chemistrykit.integrators. Three classic mechanisms -- built from its named constructors -- are each checked here against a closed-form solution, and the steady-state approximation for the consecutive chain is shown converging as the second step is made much faster than the first.
Parallel, consecutive, and reversible reaction networks

StoichiometricNetwork's general mass-action engine, applied to a three-step radical chain mechanism (initiation, branching propagation, and linear termination), reproduces the qualitative signature of a chain-branching explosion: below a critical branching rate the radical concentration stays small and the fuel decays gently, while above it the radical population grows explosively and burns through the fuel in a short, sharp spike -- exactly the ignition-vs-no-ignition switch behind Semenov's and Hinshelwood's explosion-limit theory.
Chain-branching explosions and Semenov's critical condition

Below the Hopf-bifurcation threshold (:math:`B < 1 + A^2`) the Brusselator's single fixed point is a stable focus and any initial concentration relaxes toward it. Above threshold, that same fixed point becomes unstable and every trajectory is drawn instead onto a surrounding stable limit cycle -- sustained chemical oscillation with no external forcing, driven purely by the autocatalytic X^2 Y term.

jablonski_network builds the 3-state (S1, T1, S0) Jablonski excited-state decay network as a StoichiometricNetwork -- reusing the kinetics domain's general mass-action reaction-network engine rather than reimplementing rate-equation integration. The numerical integration is checked here against jablonski_populations_analytic's closed-form solution.

A photoswitch A <-> B under simultaneous forward and reverse photolysis reaches a photostationary state (PSS) rather than running to completion. photoswitch_network reuses reversible directly, and photostationary_state gives the exact algebraic PSS composition -- checked here against direct long-time numerical integration of the ODE system.
Photostationary-state kinetics of a two-state photoswitch

free_radical_network builds the lumped initiation/propagation/termination kinetics as a StoichiometricNetwork and integrates it numerically. Because termination is much faster than initiator decomposition, the radical concentration relaxes almost immediately to the steady-state approximation's closed-form prediction (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.steady_state_radical_concentration) -- verified here by comparing the two directly -- while monomer is consumed only slowly, at the classic square-root-of-initiator rate.

free_radical_network's mode argument selects between the two ways two growing radical chains can terminate: combination (they fuse into a single dead chain) or disproportionation (one radical abstracts a hydrogen from the other, producing two separate dead chains). Bevington, Melville, and Taylor ("The Termination Reaction in Radical Polymerizations," J. Polym. Sci. 12 (1954), 449-459) showed how to distinguish the two experimentally, by end-group analysis and by the resulting degree of polymerization's relationship to the kinetic chain length (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.kinetic_chain_length) nu: \bar X_n = 2\nu for combination (two radicals' worth of monomer per dead chain) but \bar X_n = \nu for disproportionation (one radical's worth per dead chain) -- verified here directly against the numerically integrated network.

chemistrykit.LJFluid: A monatomic Lennard-Jones fluid (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LJFluid) started on a simple-cubic lattice with Maxwell-Boltzmann velocities (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LJFluid.from_lattice), integrated with no thermostat (a microcanonical, NVE run) via the shared velocity-Verlet integrator. Two standard checks: total energy should be constant to within integration error, and the radial distribution function g(r) should show liquid-like structure (a first peak near the Lennard-Jones minimum) rather than the flat g(r)=1 of an ideal gas.
An NVE Lennard-Jones fluid: energy conservation and g(r)

A direct link between chemistrykit.md and chemistrykit.statmech: molecular dynamics produces an actual ensemble of particle velocities, and statistical mechanics predicts what their distribution should look like at equilibrium. After a short equilibration run, an LJFluid's particle speeds are histogrammed and compared against chemistrykit.statmech.MaxwellBoltzmannSpeedDistribution evaluated at the simulation's own (instantaneous, measured) temperature -- no fitting involved.
Cross-checking an MD trajectory against the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution

Truncating the Lennard-Jones potential at its own minimum, r=2^{1/6}\sigma (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LennardJones.r_min), and shifting it to be continuous there removes the attractive tail entirely and leaves a purely repulsive potential -- the Weeks-Chandler-Andersen (WCA) reference system, and (in reduced units) a smoothed stand-in for a fluid of hard spheres. Comparing the radial distribution function g(r) of this purely repulsive LJFluid at low and high density shows that pronounced short-range positional order can appear from packing alone, with no attractive force anywhere in the potential -- the essential physics behind Alder and Wainwright's 1957 discovery that hard spheres alone can freeze.
Purely repulsive (WCA) particles: packing order without attraction

Starting the same Lennard-Jones fluid configuration well away from its target temperature, three runs compare how the instantaneous kinetic temperature evolves: an unthermostatted (NVE, microcanonical) run, where it simply stays wherever it started; the crude, deterministic VelocityRescalingThermostat, which snaps it back to the target at every rescaling; and the NoseHooverThermostat, which relaxes it smoothly toward the target via an extended-system friction variable.
Thermostats: NVE vs. velocity-rescaling vs. Nose-Hoover

An NVE Lennard-Jones fluid: energy conservation and g(r)

Truncating the Lennard-Jones potential at its own minimum, r=2^{1/6}\sigma (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LennardJones.r_min), and shifting it to be continuous there removes the attractive tail entirely and leaves a purely repulsive potential -- the Weeks-Chandler-Andersen (WCA) reference system, and (in reduced units) a smoothed stand-in for a fluid of hard spheres. Comparing the radial distribution function g(r) of this purely repulsive LJFluid at low and high density shows that pronounced short-range positional order can appear from packing alone, with no attractive force anywhere in the potential -- the essential physics behind Alder and Wainwright's 1957 discovery that hard spheres alone can freeze.
Purely repulsive (WCA) particles: packing order without attraction
chemistrykit.LJFluid.run: A monatomic Lennard-Jones fluid (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LJFluid) started on a simple-cubic lattice with Maxwell-Boltzmann velocities (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LJFluid.from_lattice), integrated with no thermostat (a microcanonical, NVE run) via the shared velocity-Verlet integrator. Two standard checks: total energy should be constant to within integration error, and the radial distribution function g(r) should show liquid-like structure (a first peak near the Lennard-Jones minimum) rather than the flat g(r)=1 of an ideal gas.
An NVE Lennard-Jones fluid: energy conservation and g(r)

A direct link between chemistrykit.md and chemistrykit.statmech: molecular dynamics produces an actual ensemble of particle velocities, and statistical mechanics predicts what their distribution should look like at equilibrium. After a short equilibration run, an LJFluid's particle speeds are histogrammed and compared against chemistrykit.statmech.MaxwellBoltzmannSpeedDistribution evaluated at the simulation's own (instantaneous, measured) temperature -- no fitting involved.
Cross-checking an MD trajectory against the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution

Starting the same Lennard-Jones fluid configuration well away from its target temperature, three runs compare how the instantaneous kinetic temperature evolves: an unthermostatted (NVE, microcanonical) run, where it simply stays wherever it started; the crude, deterministic VelocityRescalingThermostat, which snaps it back to the target at every rescaling; and the NoseHooverThermostat, which relaxes it smoothly toward the target via an extended-system friction variable.

chemistrykit.LangmuirFit: LangmuirIsotherm models monolayer adsorption on a fixed pool of identical surface sites. Its fractional coverage \theta=KP/(1+KP) reaches exactly one-half at the half-saturation pressure P=1/K, and fit_langmuir recovers (K, qmax) from noisy loading-vs-pressure data via the standard 1/q-vs-1/P linearization.
chemistrykit.LangmuirIsotherm: Paul Sabatier's qualitative principle -- that the best catalyst binds a reaction intermediate neither too weakly (nothing sticks long enough to react) nor too strongly (the surface clogs with product and never frees up for another turnover) -- is illustrated here with the standard modern textbook toy model (see, e.g., Chorkendorff & Niemantsverdriet, Concepts of Modern Catalysis and Kinetics, 2nd ed., Wiley-VCH, 2007, Ch. 8): a two-step surface mechanism whose overall rate needs both an occupied site (to hold the adsorbed intermediate) and an empty site (for the next step to proceed), so the rate is proportional to \theta(1-\theta), with \theta the Langmuir coverage (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.langmuir.langmuir_coverage) set by the adsorption equilibrium constant K -- a proxy for binding strength. This is not a literal reproduction of Sabatier's own (qualitative) or Balandin's (multiplet-theory) equations, just the simplest possible model with the same volcano-shaped structure they established conceptually and structurally, respectively.
The Sabatier principle and the catalytic volcano curve

chemistrykit.LatticeGasAdsorption: LatticeGasAdsorption models M independent, non-interacting adsorption sites, each either empty or occupied with binding energy \epsilon. Treating the sites in equilibrium with an ideal-gas reservoir gives exactly the Langmuir isotherm \theta=P/(P+P_0) -- shown here for two binding strengths, alongside the purely combinatorial (fixed-`N`, canonical) configurational entropy of the lattice, which is maximal at half filling.
A canonical-ensemble derivation of the Langmuir adsorption isotherm

The Buckingham (exp-6) potential replaces the Lennard-Jones r^{-12} repulsive wall with an exponential -- closer to the true quantum-mechanical electron-overlap repulsion -- while keeping the same r^{-6} dispersion attraction. Matched to a Lennard-Jones potential's well depth, position, and long-range tail, the two agree closely everywhere near and beyond the minimum. But the exponential repulsion is eventually overwhelmed by the unbounded -C/r^6 attractive term at short enough range, so the Buckingham potential has a second, spurious turnover well inside the true minimum: past that point it falls back toward -\infty as r\to0 instead of diverging to +\infty the way Lennard-Jones's pure r^{-12} repulsion does.
Buckingham vs. Lennard-Jones: exponential repulsion and its inner turnover

Otto Stern's 1920 molecular-beam apparatus gave the first direct experimental measurement of a gas's actual molecular speeds, rather than only their statistical consequences (pressure, diffusion, viscosity) -- a rotating-drum time-of-flight technique later refined by Zartman and Ko (1930-1934) into a quantitative confirmation of the full Maxwell-Boltzmann functional form, not just its mean. sample draws exactly such a synthetic "beam" of molecular speeds; binning it into a histogram and comparing it to the exact analytic pdf reproduces the kind of check Stern, and later Zartman and Ko, made directly against a real gas.
Verifying the speed distribution: Stern's molecular-beam experiment

chemistrykit.MichaelisMentenFit: Three related views of the same enzyme: the saturating Michaelis-Menten rate-vs-substrate curve, its Lineweaver-Burk double-reciprocal linearization (used to extract V_{max} and K_m from noisy initial-rate data), and how competitive vs. noncompetitive inhibition distort that curve differently.
chemistrykit.MolecularDynamicsSystem: The harmonic bond potential (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) is the small-oscillation limit of the anharmonic Morse potential -- they agree near the equilibrium separation but diverge away from it (Morse correctly flattens out toward a finite dissociation energy; harmonic does not). DiatomicOscillator integrates the classical two-body bond-vibration problem via the shared velocity-Verlet integrator, for either potential.
Morse vs. harmonic bond potentials, and diatomic bond vibration

HarmonicMolecule builds a small molecular-mechanics "force field" out of nothing but harmonic bond (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) and harmonic angle-bend (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicAngle) terms -- the classical, spring-and-hinge picture of molecular structure that founded molecular mechanics. A bent, water-like triatomic (one heavy vertex atom, two light outer atoms, equilibrium angle 104.5 degrees) is displaced away from its equilibrium geometry and left to vibrate under velocity-Verlet integration alone (no thermostat): both bond lengths and the bond angle oscillate indefinitely about their equilibrium values, and the total energy is conserved to within integration error.
A bent triatomic molecule: coupled bond-stretch and angle-bend vibrations

Comparing the radial distribution function g(r) of this purely repulsive LJFluid at low and high density shows that pronounced short-range positional order can appear from packing alone, with no attractive force anywhere in the potential -- the essential physics behind Alder and Wainwright's 1957 discovery that hard spheres alone can freeze.

HarmonicMolecule builds a small molecular-mechanics "force field" out of nothing but harmonic bond (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) and harmonic angle-bend (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicAngle) terms -- the classical, spring-and-hinge picture of molecular structure that founded molecular mechanics. A bent, water-like triatomic (one heavy vertex atom, two light outer atoms, equilibrium angle 104.5 degrees) is displaced away from its equilibrium geometry and left to vibrate under velocity-Verlet integration alone (no thermostat): both bond lengths and the bond angle oscillate indefinitely about their equilibrium values, and the total energy is conserved to within integration error.

Alfred Werner's 1893 coordination theory proposed that a six-coordinate metal complex's ligands sit at the vertices of an octahedron around the central atom -- the structural model he supported entirely through painstaking isomer-counting arguments, decades before any direct structural technique existed to see it. Sulfur hexafluoride is a main-group molecule built on exactly that same six-coordinate octahedral skeleton, and its symmetry -- four independent three-fold (C3) body- diagonal axes on top of the three obvious four-fold (C4) axes along the S-F bonds -- makes it the standard worked example for the cubic Oh point group. This also exercises the specific candidate-axis machinery (~chemistrykit.structure.utils.symmetry_ops.candidate_axes's three-way position-vector sums) needed to find those body-diagonal C3 axes at all: with the six ligands placed exactly on the cardinal axes, no pairwise combination of two ligand vectors can ever point along a body diagonal such as (1, 1, 1).

Builds four molecules spanning the five idealized electron-domain polyhedra -- methane (AX4E0, tetrahedral), water (AX2E2, bent from a tetrahedral parent), sulfur tetrafluoride (AX4E1, seesaw from a trigonal bipyramidal parent), and xenon tetrafluoride (AX4E2, square planar from an octahedral parent) -- via build_vsepr_molecule, and verifies the exact idealized bond angles each shape predicts.

Jacobus van't Hoff and Joseph Le Bel independently proposed in 1874 that a carbon atom's four bonds point toward the vertices of a regular tetrahedron -- and that a carbon bonded to four different substituents therefore has no internal mirror symmetry: its mirror image cannot be superimposed on itself by any rotation, giving two distinct, non- interconvertible molecules (enantiomers). This builds a genuinely tetrahedral AX4 center -- bromochlorofluoromethane, CHFClBr, the textbook minimal chiral carbon -- from domain_positions's real 3D vertex coordinates, confirms the exact 109.47-degree bond angles van't Hoff and Le Bel's model predicts, and then demonstrates the chirality itself numerically: a scalar-triple-product handedness invariant flips sign under reflection but is exactly preserved under any proper rotation (built with rotation_matrix), so no rotation can ever turn the molecule into its own mirror image.

The Buckingham (exp-6) potential replaces the Lennard-Jones r^{-12} repulsive wall with an exponential -- closer to the true quantum-mechanical electron-overlap repulsion -- while keeping the same r^{-6} dispersion attraction. Matched to a Lennard-Jones potential's well depth, position, and long-range tail, the two agree closely everywhere near and beyond the minimum. But the exponential repulsion is eventually overwhelmed by the unbounded -C/r^6 attractive term at short enough range, so the Buckingham potential has a second, spurious turnover well inside the true minimum: past that point it falls back toward -\infty as r\to0 instead of diverging to +\infty the way Lennard-Jones's pure r^{-12} repulsion does.

chemistrykit.PartitionFunction.from_wave: VibrationalPartitionFunctionHarmonic's heat capacity is the Einstein-oscillator formula: it vanishes as T\to0 (the vibration is "frozen out") and approaches the classical equipartition value k_B per mode as T\to\infty. Separately, sackur_tetrode_entropy gives the translational entropy of an ideal gas directly from its molecular mass, temperature, and pressure -- checked here against the standard tabulated value for argon.
The Einstein vibrational heat capacity, and Sackur-Tetrode entropy

James Clerk Maxwell (1860) and, in fully general form, Ludwig Boltzmann (1871) showed that every classical quadratic degree of freedom of a system in thermal equilibrium contributes exactly \frac12k_B to its heat capacity -- the equipartition theorem. A rigid diatomic molecule therefore "should" carry \frac32k_B (translation) + k_B (2 rotational degrees of freedom) + k_B (1 vibrational mode, kinetic + potential) = \frac72k_B at every temperature -- a prediction 19th-century equipartition theory could not explain deviations from (Maxwell himself flagged the puzzle sharply in 1879). Only VibrationalPartitionFunctionHarmonic is an exact quantum treatment in this package, so it alone shows the real resolution Einstein gave in 1907: a mode's contribution only "switches on" once k_BT exceeds its own quantum spacing. RotationalPartitionFunctionLinear, by contrast, implements only the classical high-temperature limit (as its own docstring flags), so it contributes its full k_B at every temperature here -- a deliberate approximation, harmless in practice because real rotational spacings are tiny compared to vibrational ones (as the numbers below confirm), but worth seeing explicitly rather than assuming.
The equipartition theorem, and why only one mode actually "freezes out"

chemistrykit.RotationalPartitionFunction: James Clerk Maxwell (1860) and, in fully general form, Ludwig Boltzmann (1871) showed that every classical quadratic degree of freedom of a system in thermal equilibrium contributes exactly \frac12k_B to its heat capacity -- the equipartition theorem. A rigid diatomic molecule therefore "should" carry \frac32k_B (translation) + k_B (2 rotational degrees of freedom) + k_B (1 vibrational mode, kinetic + potential) = \frac72k_B at every temperature -- a prediction 19th-century equipartition theory could not explain deviations from (Maxwell himself flagged the puzzle sharply in 1879). Only VibrationalPartitionFunctionHarmonic is an exact quantum treatment in this package, so it alone shows the real resolution Einstein gave in 1907: a mode's contribution only "switches on" once k_BT exceeds its own quantum spacing. RotationalPartitionFunctionLinear, by contrast, implements only the classical high-temperature limit (as its own docstring flags), so it contributes its full k_B at every temperature here -- a deliberate approximation, harmless in practice because real rotational spacings are tiny compared to vibrational ones (as the numbers below confirm), but worth seeing explicitly rather than assuming.
The equipartition theorem, and why only one mode actually "freezes out"

chemistrykit.Spectrum: Builds a vibronic progression from the Huang-Rhys displacement parameter, verifies the Franck-Condon factors' normalization (they must sum to 1 -- the required correctness check for any Franck-Condon calculation), and shows how a larger excited-state displacement shifts the most-intense vibronic peak to higher v'.

Simulates ethanol's classic -CH3 triplet and -CH2- quartet (each proton set split only by its 3-bond neighbor, the textbook first-order pattern), then a genuine doublet of triplets from two chemically distinct coupling partners with different J values.

Builds an HCl-like rigid rotor from chemistrykit.quantum, predicts its rotational-spectrum line positions and relative (Boltzmann-weighted) intensities, and shows how substituting deuterium for hydrogen shifts every line -- the standard way isotopic substitution is used to confirm a rotational-spectrum assignment.

Predicts HCl's fundamental IR absorption from a harmonic oscillator, compares it against the exact (anharmonic) Morse-potential fundamental and first overtone, then inverts the observed 0\to1/0\to2 band positions to recover the spectroscopic constants \omega_e/\omega_ex_e -- exactly the way real anharmonicity constants are measured from an observed overtone spectrum.

chemistrykit.SternVolmerFit: stern_volmer_ratio gives the linear intensity-ratio-vs-quencher-concentration relationship; fit_stern_volmer recovers the Stern-Volmer constant from synthetic data. chemistrykit.StoichiometricNetwork: StoichiometricNetwork integrates an arbitrary mass-action reaction network numerically via chemistrykit.integrators. Three classic mechanisms -- built from its named constructors -- are each checked here against a closed-form solution, and the steady-state approximation for the consecutive chain is shown converging as the second step is made much faster than the first.
Parallel, consecutive, and reversible reaction networks

StoichiometricNetwork's general mass-action engine, applied to a three-step radical chain mechanism (initiation, branching propagation, and linear termination), reproduces the qualitative signature of a chain-branching explosion: below a critical branching rate the radical concentration stays small and the fuel decays gently, while above it the radical population grows explosively and burns through the fuel in a short, sharp spike -- exactly the ignition-vs-no-ignition switch behind Semenov's and Hinshelwood's explosion-limit theory.
Chain-branching explosions and Semenov's critical condition

jablonski_network builds the 3-state (S1, T1, S0) Jablonski excited-state decay network as a StoichiometricNetwork -- reusing the kinetics domain's general mass-action reaction-network engine rather than reimplementing rate-equation integration. The numerical integration is checked here against jablonski_populations_analytic's closed-form solution.

A photoswitch A <-> B under simultaneous forward and reverse photolysis reaches a photostationary state (PSS) rather than running to completion. photoswitch_network reuses reversible directly, and photostationary_state gives the exact algebraic PSS composition -- checked here against direct long-time numerical integration of the ODE system.
Photostationary-state kinetics of a two-state photoswitch

free_radical_network builds the lumped initiation/propagation/termination kinetics as a StoichiometricNetwork and integrates it numerically. Because termination is much faster than initiator decomposition, the radical concentration relaxes almost immediately to the steady-state approximation's closed-form prediction (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.steady_state_radical_concentration) -- verified here by comparing the two directly -- while monomer is consumed only slowly, at the classic square-root-of-initiator rate.

Walter Heitler and Fritz London's 1927 quantum-mechanical treatment of H2 -- the paper usually credited with founding quantum chemistry as a field -- showed for the first time why two hydrogen atoms bind: the symmetric (in-phase) combination of their two atomic orbitals builds up electron density in the region between the nuclei, lowering the energy below that of the separated atoms, while the antisymmetric (out-of-phase) combination depletes density there and raises the energy instead. Their original calculation used two-electron integrals this package does not implement (chemistrykit.quantum.utils.basis_sets stops at the one-electron integrals H2PlusVariational needs for H2+), but the same qualitative physics -- constructive vs. destructive interference of atomic orbitals along the bond axis -- is exactly what H2+'s own bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals show, using the genuine LCAO coefficients solve computes, not an assumed equal-weight combination.
Heitler-London's insight: bonding vs. antibonding electron density
chemistrykit.VariationalSolver.cyclic_po: Builds the Huckel secular matrix for butadiene and benzene (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.HuckelSystem), diagonalizes it via numpy.linalg.eigh (a genuine eigenvalue problem, not a lookup table), cross-checks the result against the closed-form Coulson/Frost eigenvalue formulas, and checks Huckel's 4n+2 rule (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.is_aromatic_by_huckel_rule) against the computed spectrum's degeneracies.
Huckel theory: butadiene, benzene, and the 4n+2 aromaticity rule

Two independent routes to a (generally non-integer) bond order: Pauling's empirical bond-length correlation applied to benzene's intermediate C-C bond length, and the Coulson bond order computed directly from Huckel molecular-orbital coefficients for the same molecule -- the two independent methods agree that benzene's C-C bond order sits between 1 and 2.

chemistrykit.VelocityRescalingThermostat: Truncating the Lennard-Jones potential at its own minimum, r=2^{1/6}\sigma (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LennardJones.r_min), and shifting it to be continuous there removes the attractive tail entirely and leaves a purely repulsive potential -- the Weeks-Chandler-Andersen (WCA) reference system, and (in reduced units) a smoothed stand-in for a fluid of hard spheres. Comparing the radial distribution function g(r) of this purely repulsive LJFluid at low and high density shows that pronounced short-range positional order can appear from packing alone, with no attractive force anywhere in the potential -- the essential physics behind Alder and Wainwright's 1957 discovery that hard spheres alone can freeze.
Purely repulsive (WCA) particles: packing order without attraction

Starting the same Lennard-Jones fluid configuration well away from its target temperature, three runs compare how the instantaneous kinetic temperature evolves: an unthermostatted (NVE, microcanonical) run, where it simply stays wherever it started; the crude, deterministic VelocityRescalingThermostat, which snaps it back to the target at every rescaling; and the NoseHooverThermostat, which relaxes it smoothly toward the target via an extended-system friction variable.
Thermostats: NVE vs. velocity-rescaling vs. Nose-Hoover
chemistrykit.VibrationalPartitionFunctio: VibrationalPartitionFunctionHarmonic's heat capacity is the Einstein-oscillator formula: it vanishes as T\to0 (the vibration is "frozen out") and approaches the classical equipartition value k_B per mode as T\to\infty. Separately, sackur_tetrode_entropy gives the translational entropy of an ideal gas directly from its molecular mass, temperature, and pressure -- checked here against the standard tabulated value for argon.
The Einstein vibrational heat capacity, and Sackur-Tetrode entropy

James Clerk Maxwell (1860) and, in fully general form, Ludwig Boltzmann (1871) showed that every classical quadratic degree of freedom of a system in thermal equilibrium contributes exactly \frac12k_B to its heat capacity -- the equipartition theorem. A rigid diatomic molecule therefore "should" carry \frac32k_B (translation) + k_B (2 rotational degrees of freedom) + k_B (1 vibrational mode, kinetic + potential) = \frac72k_B at every temperature -- a prediction 19th-century equipartition theory could not explain deviations from (Maxwell himself flagged the puzzle sharply in 1879). Only VibrationalPartitionFunctionHarmonic is an exact quantum treatment in this package, so it alone shows the real resolution Einstein gave in 1907: a mode's contribution only "switches on" once k_BT exceeds its own quantum spacing. RotationalPartitionFunctionLinear, by contrast, implements only the classical high-temperature limit (as its own docstring flags), so it contributes its full k_B at every temperature here -- a deliberate approximation, harmless in practice because real rotational spacings are tiny compared to vibrational ones (as the numbers below confirm), but worth seeing explicitly rather than assuming.
The equipartition theorem, and why only one mode actually "freezes out"

chemistrykit.WeakAcid: Dissolving less acid in more water increases the percentage of it that dissociates, even though the absolute [H^+] goes down -- the Ostwald dilution law, here from the exact cubic charge-balance solution in WeakAcid rather than the more commonly taught \sqrt{K_aC_a} approximation. Also: designing a buffer for a target pH with from_target_ph.
The Ostwald dilution law and buffer design
chemistrykit.WeakAcidStrongBaseTitration: Three different titration types -- acid-base (pH, chemistrykit.solutions.systems.titration), redox (electrode potential E, RedoxTitration), and complexometric (`pM`, EDTATitration) -- all share the same qualitative S-shaped curve, and the same numerical equivalence-point detector (steepest response change).
Acid-base, redox, and EDTA titration curves side by side

Comparing a strong-acid/strong-base titration (~chemistrykit.solutions.systems.titration.StrongAcidStrongBaseTitration) against a weak-acid/strong-base titration (~chemistrykit.solutions.systems.titration.WeakAcidStrongBaseTitration) of the same concentrations: the weak-acid curve starts at a higher pH, has a buffer region around its half-equivalence point (where pH = pKa), and its equivalence point is basic rather than neutral -- all visible directly from the curve shapes.

chemistrykit.XRDPeak: powder_xrd_peaks computes each reflection's structure factor (~chemistrykit.crystal.systems.xrd.structure_factor) directly from atomic positions and Miller indices, so BCC's and FCC's systematic absences (reflections with zero intensity by symmetry) fall out automatically rather than being hardcoded as a rule.

chemistrykit.ZeroOrder: The three textbook elementary rate laws -- ZeroOrder, FirstOrder, and SecondOrder -- all started from the same initial concentration and with rate constants chosen to give the same half-life, so the different curvature (linear, exponential, hyperbolic) is the only thing distinguishing them. First order is the only one whose half-life doesn't depend on the starting concentration; the plot below marks all three half-lives to make that concrete.
Zero-, first-, and second-order integrated rate laws

chemistrykit.constants.ELECTRONVOLT: H2PlusVariational builds the 2x2 Hamiltonian and overlap matrices for a minimal one-Gaussian- per-proton basis, solves the secular equation HC=SCE, and then variationally optimizes the shared Gaussian exponent -- a genuine application of the Rayleigh-Ritz variational theorem: minimizing over a real parameter can only lower (never raise) the computed energy toward the true ground state.
H2+ in a minimal 2-Gaussian basis: the variational principle at work

HydrogenLikeAtom reproduces the textbook 13.6 eV hydrogen ground-state energy exactly, and its radial wavefunctions (built from the associated Laguerre polynomials of scipy.special) are independently checked here by numerically integrating them to a normalized probability of 1.
Hydrogen radial wavefunctions and orbital energies
chemistrykit.constants.HBAR: Checks quartic_perturbation_first_order_correction's first-order Rayleigh-Schrodinger estimate against exact numerical diagonalization of the full anharmonic Hamiltonian (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.perturbation.anharmonic_energy_levels, built in a truncated harmonic-oscillator basis via position_operator_matrix), and confirms that a cubic perturbation gives exactly zero first-order correction by parity.
Perturbation theory vs. exact diagonalization for the quartic oscillator
chemistrykit.constants.R: For N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2, this plots the total Gibbs energy of the reacting mixture as a function of the extent of reaction \xi and shows that solve_equilibrium_composition's answer sits exactly at the minimum -- the numerical method actually doing what its name says. It also shows a van't Hoff plot (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.equilibrium.fit_van_t_hoff) recovering a reaction's enthalpy from synthetic equilibrium-constant-vs- temperature data.
Gibbs-energy minimization and the van't Hoff equation

chemistrykit.electrochem.BatteryDischarg: ConstantCurrentBattery is a deliberately simplified constant-current discharge model (see its docstring for exactly what is and is not captured). This example shows the ideal (Peukert exponent k=1) case delivering the same effective capacity at every discharge rate, and a more realistic k>1 case showing the familiar "faster discharge delivers less total capacity" effect.
A simplified constant-current battery discharge model, and Peukert's law

chemistrykit.electrochem.HalfReaction: faradays_law_mass gives the mass of a species deposited or consumed by a constant current over time. nernst_potential relates a cell's potential under non-standard conditions to its standard potential and reaction quotient. Finally, nernst_potential_with_activity shows how Debye-Huckel activity-coefficient corrections (reused from chemistrykit.solutions.systems.activity) pull the cell potential away from the ideal, unit-activity-coefficient prediction as ionic strength grows.

StoichiometricNetwork's general mass-action engine, applied to a three-step radical chain mechanism (initiation, branching propagation, and linear termination), reproduces the qualitative signature of a chain-branching explosion: below a critical branching rate the radical concentration stays small and the fuel decays gently, while above it the radical population grows explosively and burns through the fuel in a short, sharp spike -- exactly the ignition-vs-no-ignition switch behind Semenov's and Hinshelwood's explosion-limit theory.

jablonski_network builds the 3-state (S1, T1, S0) Jablonski excited-state decay network as a StoichiometricNetwork -- reusing the kinetics domain's general mass-action reaction-network engine rather than reimplementing rate-equation integration. The numerical integration is checked here against jablonski_populations_analytic's closed-form solution.

A photoswitch A <-> B under simultaneous forward and reverse photolysis reaches a photostationary state (PSS) rather than running to completion. photoswitch_network reuses reversible directly, and photostationary_state gives the exact algebraic PSS composition -- checked here against direct long-time numerical integration of the ODE system.
Photostationary-state kinetics of a two-state photoswitch

free_radical_network builds the lumped initiation/propagation/termination kinetics as a StoichiometricNetwork and integrates it numerically. Because termination is much faster than initiator decomposition, the radical concentration relaxes almost immediately to the steady-state approximation's closed-form prediction (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.steady_state_radical_concentration) -- verified here by comparing the two directly -- while monomer is consumed only slowly, at the classic square-root-of-initiator rate.

free_radical_network's mode argument selects between the two ways two growing radical chains can terminate: combination (they fuse into a single dead chain) or disproportionation (one radical abstracts a hydrogen from the other, producing two separate dead chains). Bevington, Melville, and Taylor ("The Termination Reaction in Radical Polymerizations," J. Polym. Sci. 12 (1954), 449-459) showed how to distinguish the two experimentally, by end-group analysis and by the resulting degree of polymerization's relationship to the kinetic chain length (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.kinetic_chain_length) nu: \bar X_n = 2\nu for combination (two radicals' worth of monomer per dead chain) but \bar X_n = \nu for disproportionation (one radical's worth per dead chain) -- verified here directly against the numerically integrated network.

Below the Hopf-bifurcation threshold (:math:`B < 1 + A^2`) the Brusselator's single fixed point is a stable focus and any initial concentration relaxes toward it. Above threshold, that same fixed point becomes unstable and every trajectory is drawn instead onto a surrounding stable limit cycle -- sustained chemical oscillation with no external forcing, driven purely by the autocatalytic X^2 Y term.
chemistrykit.kinetics.ReactionNetwork.co: StoichiometricNetwork integrates an arbitrary mass-action reaction network numerically via chemistrykit.integrators. Three classic mechanisms -- built from its named constructors -- are each checked here against a closed-form solution, and the steady-state approximation for the consecutive chain is shown converging as the second step is made much faster than the first.

jablonski_network builds the 3-state (S1, T1, S0) Jablonski excited-state decay network as a StoichiometricNetwork -- reusing the kinetics domain's general mass-action reaction-network engine rather than reimplementing rate-equation integration. A photoswitch A <-> B under simultaneous forward and reverse photolysis reaches a photostationary state (PSS) rather than running to completion. photoswitch_network reuses reversible directly, and photostationary_state gives the exact algebraic PSS composition -- checked here against direct long-time numerical integration of the ODE system.
Photostationary-state kinetics of a two-state photoswitch

free_radical_network builds the lumped initiation/propagation/termination kinetics as a StoichiometricNetwork and integrates it numerically. Because termination is much faster than initiator decomposition, the radical concentration relaxes almost immediately to the steady-state approximation's closed-form prediction (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.steady_state_radical_concentration) -- verified here by comparing the two directly -- while monomer is consumed only slowly, at the classic square-root-of-initiator rate.

free_radical_network's mode argument selects between the two ways two growing radical chains can terminate: combination (they fuse into a single dead chain) or disproportionation (one radical abstracts a hydrogen from the other, producing two separate dead chains). Bevington, Melville, and Taylor ("The Termination Reaction in Radical Polymerizations," J. Polym. Sci. 12 (1954), 449-459) showed how to distinguish the two experimentally, by end-group analysis and by the resulting degree of polymerization's relationship to the kinetic chain length (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.kinetic_chain_length) nu: \bar X_n = 2\nu for combination (two radicals' worth of monomer per dead chain) but \bar X_n = \nu for disproportionation (one radical's worth per dead chain) -- verified here directly against the numerically integrated network.

chemistrykit.md.Buckingham: The Buckingham (exp-6) potential replaces the Lennard-Jones r^{-12} repulsive wall with an exponential -- closer to the true quantum-mechanical electron-overlap repulsion -- while keeping the same r^{-6} dispersion attraction. Matched to a Lennard-Jones potential's well depth, position, and long-range tail, the two agree closely everywhere near and beyond the minimum. But the exponential repulsion is eventually overwhelmed by the unbounded -C/r^6 attractive term at short enough range, so the Buckingham potential has a second, spurious turnover well inside the true minimum: past that point it falls back toward -\infty as r\to0 instead of diverging to +\infty the way Lennard-Jones's pure r^{-12} repulsion does.
Buckingham vs. Lennard-Jones: exponential repulsion and its inner turnover

chemistrykit.md.HarmonicMolecule: HarmonicMolecule builds a small molecular-mechanics "force field" out of nothing but harmonic bond (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) and harmonic angle-bend (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicAngle) terms -- the classical, spring-and-hinge picture of molecular structure that founded molecular mechanics. A direct link between chemistrykit.md and chemistrykit.statmech: molecular dynamics produces an actual ensemble of particle velocities, and statistical mechanics predicts what their distribution should look like at equilibrium. After a short equilibration run, an LJFluid's particle speeds are histogrammed and compared against chemistrykit.statmech.MaxwellBoltzmannSpeedDistribution evaluated at the simulation's own (instantaneous, measured) temperature -- no fitting involved.
Cross-checking an MD trajectory against the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution

Truncating the Lennard-Jones potential at its own minimum, r=2^{1/6}\sigma (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LennardJones.r_min), and shifting it to be continuous there removes the attractive tail entirely and leaves a purely repulsive potential -- the Weeks-Chandler-Andersen (WCA) reference system, and (in reduced units) a smoothed stand-in for a fluid of hard spheres. Comparing the radial distribution function g(r) of this purely repulsive LJFluid at low and high density shows that pronounced short-range positional order can appear from packing alone, with no attractive force anywhere in the potential -- the essential physics behind Alder and Wainwright's 1957 discovery that hard spheres alone can freeze.
Purely repulsive (WCA) particles: packing order without attraction

Starting the same Lennard-Jones fluid configuration well away from its target temperature, three runs compare how the instantaneous kinetic temperature evolves: an unthermostatted (NVE, microcanonical) run, where it simply stays wherever it started; the crude, deterministic VelocityRescalingThermostat, which snaps it back to the target at every rescaling; and the NoseHooverThermostat, which relaxes it smoothly toward the target via an extended-system friction variable.

The Buckingham (exp-6) potential replaces the Lennard-Jones r^{-12} repulsive wall with an exponential -- closer to the true quantum-mechanical electron-overlap repulsion -- while keeping the same r^{-6} dispersion attraction. Matched to a Lennard-Jones potential's well depth, position, and long-range tail, the two agree closely everywhere near and beyond the minimum. But the exponential repulsion is eventually overwhelmed by the unbounded -C/r^6 attractive term at short enough range, so the Buckingham potential has a second, spurious turnover well inside the true minimum: past that point it falls back toward -\infty as r\to0 instead of diverging to +\infty the way Lennard-Jones's pure r^{-12} repulsion does.
Buckingham vs. Lennard-Jones: exponential repulsion and its inner turnover

But the exponential repulsion is eventually overwhelmed by the unbounded -C/r^6 attractive term at short enough range, so the Buckingham potential has a second, spurious turnover well inside the true minimum: past that point it falls back toward -\infty as r\to0 instead of diverging to +\infty the way Lennard-Jones's pure r^{-12} repulsion does.
Buckingham vs. Lennard-Jones: exponential repulsion and its inner turnover
chemistrykit.md.VelocityRescalingThermos: Truncating the Lennard-Jones potential at its own minimum, r=2^{1/6}\sigma (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LennardJones.r_min), and shifting it to be continuous there removes the attractive tail entirely and leaves a purely repulsive potential -- the Weeks-Chandler-Andersen (WCA) reference system, and (in reduced units) a smoothed stand-in for a fluid of hard spheres. Comparing the radial distribution function g(r) of this purely repulsive LJFluid at low and high density shows that pronounced short-range positional order can appear from packing alone, with no attractive force anywhere in the potential -- the essential physics behind Alder and Wainwright's 1957 discovery that hard spheres alone can freeze.
Purely repulsive (WCA) particles: packing order without attraction

Starting the same Lennard-Jones fluid configuration well away from its target temperature, three runs compare how the instantaneous kinetic temperature evolves: an unthermostatted (NVE, microcanonical) run, where it simply stays wherever it started; the crude, deterministic VelocityRescalingThermostat, which snaps it back to the target at every rescaling; and the NoseHooverThermostat, which relaxes it smoothly toward the target via an extended-system friction variable.
Thermostats: NVE vs. velocity-rescaling vs. Nose-Hoover
chemistrykit.md.core.MDResult: A monatomic Lennard-Jones fluid (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LJFluid) started on a simple-cubic lattice with Maxwell-Boltzmann velocities (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LJFluid.from_lattice), integrated with no thermostat (a microcanonical, NVE run) via the shared velocity-Verlet integrator. Two standard checks: total energy should be constant to within integration error, and the radial distribution function g(r) should show liquid-like structure (a first peak near the Lennard-Jones minimum) rather than the flat g(r)=1 of an ideal gas.
An NVE Lennard-Jones fluid: energy conservation and g(r)

chemistrykit.md.core.MolecularDynamicsSy: The harmonic bond potential (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) is the small-oscillation limit of the anharmonic Morse potential -- they agree near the equilibrium separation but diverge away from it (Morse correctly flattens out toward a finite dissociation energy; harmonic does not). DiatomicOscillator integrates the classical two-body bond-vibration problem via the shared velocity-Verlet integrator, for either potential.
Morse vs. harmonic bond potentials, and diatomic bond vibration

HarmonicMolecule builds a small molecular-mechanics "force field" out of nothing but harmonic bond (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) and harmonic angle-bend (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicAngle) terms -- the classical, spring-and-hinge picture of molecular structure that founded molecular mechanics. A bent, water-like triatomic (one heavy vertex atom, two light outer atoms, equilibrium angle 104.5 degrees) is displaced away from its equilibrium geometry and left to vibrate under velocity-Verlet integration alone (no thermostat): both bond lengths and the bond angle oscillate indefinitely about their equilibrium values, and the total energy is conserved to within integration error.
A bent triatomic molecule: coupled bond-stretch and angle-bend vibrations

The harmonic bond potential (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) is the small-oscillation limit of the anharmonic Morse potential -- they agree near the equilibrium separation but diverge away from it (Morse correctly flattens out toward a finite dissociation energy; harmonic does not). DiatomicOscillator integrates the classical two-body bond-vibration problem via the shared velocity-Verlet integrator, for either potential.
Morse vs. harmonic bond potentials, and diatomic bond vibration

The Buckingham (exp-6) potential replaces the Lennard-Jones r^{-12} repulsive wall with an exponential -- closer to the true quantum-mechanical electron-overlap repulsion -- while keeping the same r^{-6} dispersion attraction. Matched to a Lennard-Jones potential's well depth, position, and long-range tail, the two agree closely everywhere near and beyond the minimum. But the exponential repulsion is eventually overwhelmed by the unbounded -C/r^6 attractive term at short enough range, so the Buckingham potential has a second, spurious turnover well inside the true minimum: past that point it falls back toward -\infty as r\to0 instead of diverging to +\infty the way Lennard-Jones's pure r^{-12} repulsion does.
Buckingham vs. Lennard-Jones: exponential repulsion and its inner turnover

chemistrykit.md.systems.HarmonicMolecule: HarmonicMolecule builds a small molecular-mechanics "force field" out of nothing but harmonic bond (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) and harmonic angle-bend (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicAngle) terms -- the classical, spring-and-hinge picture of molecular structure that founded molecular mechanics. A bent, water-like triatomic (one heavy vertex atom, two light outer atoms, equilibrium angle 104.5 degrees) is displaced away from its equilibrium geometry and left to vibrate under velocity-Verlet integration alone (no thermostat): both bond lengths and the bond angle oscillate indefinitely about their equilibrium values, and the total energy is conserved to within integration error.
A bent triatomic molecule: coupled bond-stretch and angle-bend vibrations

The Buckingham (exp-6) potential replaces the Lennard-Jones r^{-12} repulsive wall with an exponential -- closer to the true quantum-mechanical electron-overlap repulsion -- while keeping the same r^{-6} dispersion attraction. Matched to a Lennard-Jones potential's well depth, position, and long-range tail, the two agree closely everywhere near and beyond the minimum. But the exponential repulsion is eventually overwhelmed by the unbounded -C/r^6 attractive term at short enough range, so the Buckingham potential has a second, spurious turnover well inside the true minimum: past that point it falls back toward -\infty as r\to0 instead of diverging to +\infty the way Lennard-Jones's pure r^{-12} repulsion does.
Buckingham vs. Lennard-Jones: exponential repulsion and its inner turnover

The harmonic bond potential (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) is the small-oscillation limit of the anharmonic Morse potential -- they agree near the equilibrium separation but diverge away from it (Morse correctly flattens out toward a finite dissociation energy; harmonic does not). DiatomicOscillator integrates the classical two-body bond-vibration problem via the shared velocity-Verlet integrator, for either potential.

HarmonicMolecule builds a small molecular-mechanics "force field" out of nothing but harmonic bond (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) and harmonic angle-bend (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicAngle) terms -- the classical, spring-and-hinge picture of molecular structure that founded molecular mechanics. A bent, water-like triatomic (one heavy vertex atom, two light outer atoms, equilibrium angle 104.5 degrees) is displaced away from its equilibrium geometry and left to vibrate under velocity-Verlet integration alone (no thermostat): both bond lengths and the bond angle oscillate indefinitely about their equilibrium values, and the total energy is conserved to within integration error.
A bent triatomic molecule: coupled bond-stretch and angle-bend vibrations

chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growt: free_radical_network builds the lumped initiation/propagation/termination kinetics as a StoichiometricNetwork and integrates it numerically. Because termination is much faster than initiator decomposition, the radical concentration relaxes almost immediately to the steady-state approximation's closed-form prediction (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.steady_state_radical_concentration) -- verified here by comparing the two directly -- while monomer is consumed only slowly, at the classic square-root-of-initiator rate.

free_radical_network's mode argument selects between the two ways two growing radical chains can terminate: combination (they fuse into a single dead chain) or disproportionation (one radical abstracts a hydrogen from the other, producing two separate dead chains). Bevington, Melville, and Taylor ("The Termination Reaction in Radical Polymerizations," J. Polym. Sci. 12 (1954), 449-459) showed how to distinguish the two experimentally, by end-group analysis and by the resulting degree of polymerization's relationship to the kinetic chain length (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.kinetic_chain_length) nu: \bar X_n = 2\nu for combination (two radicals' worth of monomer per dead chain) but \bar X_n = \nu for disproportionation (one radical's worth per dead chain) -- verified here directly against the numerically integrated network.

free_radical_network builds the lumped initiation/propagation/termination kinetics as a StoichiometricNetwork and integrates it numerically. Because termination is much faster than initiator decomposition, the radical concentration relaxes almost immediately to the steady-state approximation's closed-form prediction (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.steady_state_radical_concentration) -- verified here by comparing the two directly -- while monomer is consumed only slowly, at the classic square-root-of-initiator rate.

free_radical_network's mode argument selects between the two ways two growing radical chains can terminate: combination (they fuse into a single dead chain) or disproportionation (one radical abstracts a hydrogen from the other, producing two separate dead chains). Bevington, Melville, and Taylor ("The Termination Reaction in Radical Polymerizations," J. Polym. Sci. 12 (1954), 449-459) showed how to distinguish the two experimentally, by end-group analysis and by the resulting degree of polymerization's relationship to the kinetic chain length (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.kinetic_chain_length) nu: \bar X_n = 2\nu for combination (two radicals' worth of monomer per dead chain) but \bar X_n = \nu for disproportionation (one radical's worth per dead chain) -- verified here directly against the numerically integrated network.

chemistrykit.quantum.EigenstateResult: H2PlusVariational builds the 2x2 Hamiltonian and overlap matrices for a minimal one-Gaussian- per-proton basis, solves the secular equation HC=SCE, and then variationally optimizes the shared Gaussian exponent -- a genuine application of the Rayleigh-Ritz variational theorem: minimizing over a real parameter can only lower (never raise) the computed energy toward the true ground state.
H2+ in a minimal 2-Gaussian basis: the variational principle at work

Walter Heitler and Fritz London's 1927 quantum-mechanical treatment of H2 -- the paper usually credited with founding quantum chemistry as a field -- showed for the first time why two hydrogen atoms bind: the symmetric (in-phase) combination of their two atomic orbitals builds up electron density in the region between the nuclei, lowering the energy below that of the separated atoms, while the antisymmetric (out-of-phase) combination depletes density there and raises the energy instead. Their original calculation used two-electron integrals this package does not implement (chemistrykit.quantum.utils.basis_sets stops at the one-electron integrals H2PlusVariational needs for H2+), but the same qualitative physics -- constructive vs. destructive interference of atomic orbitals along the bond axis -- is exactly what H2+'s own bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals show, using the genuine LCAO coefficients solve computes, not an assumed equal-weight combination.
Heitler-London's insight: bonding vs. antibonding electron density

Builds the Huckel secular matrix for butadiene and benzene (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.HuckelSystem), diagonalizes it via numpy.linalg.eigh (a genuine eigenvalue problem, not a lookup table), cross-checks the result against the closed-form Coulson/Frost eigenvalue formulas, and checks Huckel's 4n+2 rule (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.is_aromatic_by_huckel_rule) against the computed spectrum's degeneracies.
Huckel theory: butadiene, benzene, and the 4n+2 aromaticity rule

Two independent routes to a (generally non-integer) bond order: Pauling's empirical bond-length correlation applied to benzene's intermediate C-C bond length, and the Coulson bond order computed directly from Huckel molecular-orbital coefficients for the same molecule -- the two independent methods agree that benzene's C-C bond order sits between 1 and 2.

chemistrykit.quantum.VariationalSolver: H2PlusVariational builds the 2x2 Hamiltonian and overlap matrices for a minimal one-Gaussian- per-proton basis, solves the secular equation HC=SCE, and then variationally optimizes the shared Gaussian exponent -- a genuine application of the Rayleigh-Ritz variational theorem: minimizing over a real parameter can only lower (never raise) the computed energy toward the true ground state.
H2+ in a minimal 2-Gaussian basis: the variational principle at work

Walter Heitler and Fritz London's 1927 quantum-mechanical treatment of H2 -- the paper usually credited with founding quantum chemistry as a field -- showed for the first time why two hydrogen atoms bind: the symmetric (in-phase) combination of their two atomic orbitals builds up electron density in the region between the nuclei, lowering the energy below that of the separated atoms, while the antisymmetric (out-of-phase) combination depletes density there and raises the energy instead. Their original calculation used two-electron integrals this package does not implement (chemistrykit.quantum.utils.basis_sets stops at the one-electron integrals H2PlusVariational needs for H2+), but the same qualitative physics -- constructive vs. destructive interference of atomic orbitals along the bond axis -- is exactly what H2+'s own bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals show, using the genuine LCAO coefficients solve computes, not an assumed equal-weight combination.
Heitler-London's insight: bonding vs. antibonding electron density
chemistrykit.quantum.VariationalSolver.c: Builds the Huckel secular matrix for butadiene and benzene (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.HuckelSystem), diagonalizes it via numpy.linalg.eigh (a genuine eigenvalue problem, not a lookup table), cross-checks the result against the closed-form Coulson/Frost eigenvalue formulas, and checks Huckel's 4n+2 rule (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.is_aromatic_by_huckel_rule) against the computed spectrum's degeneracies.
Huckel theory: butadiene, benzene, and the 4n+2 aromaticity rule

Two independent routes to a (generally non-integer) bond order: Pauling's empirical bond-length correlation applied to benzene's intermediate C-C bond length, and the Coulson bond order computed directly from Huckel molecular-orbital coefficients for the same molecule -- the two independent methods agree that benzene's C-C bond order sits between 1 and 2.

H2PlusVariational builds the 2x2 Hamiltonian and overlap matrices for a minimal one-Gaussian- per-proton basis, solves the secular equation HC=SCE, and then variationally optimizes the shared Gaussian exponent -- a genuine application of the Rayleigh-Ritz variational theorem: minimizing over a real parameter can only lower (never raise) the computed energy toward the true ground state.
H2+ in a minimal 2-Gaussian basis: the variational principle at work

Walter Heitler and Fritz London's 1927 quantum-mechanical treatment of H2 -- the paper usually credited with founding quantum chemistry as a field -- showed for the first time why two hydrogen atoms bind: the symmetric (in-phase) combination of their two atomic orbitals builds up electron density in the region between the nuclei, lowering the energy below that of the separated atoms, while the antisymmetric (out-of-phase) combination depletes density there and raises the energy instead. Their original calculation used two-electron integrals this package does not implement (chemistrykit.quantum.utils.basis_sets stops at the one-electron integrals H2PlusVariational needs for H2+), but the same qualitative physics -- constructive vs. destructive interference of atomic orbitals along the bond axis -- is exactly what H2+'s own bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals show, using the genuine LCAO coefficients solve computes, not an assumed equal-weight combination.
Heitler-London's insight: bonding vs. antibonding electron density

Particle-in-a-box wavefunctions, cubic-box degeneracy, and dye color

chemistrykit.quantum.systems.hartree_foc: H2PlusVariational builds the 2x2 Hamiltonian and overlap matrices for a minimal one-Gaussian- per-proton basis, solves the secular equation HC=SCE, and then variationally optimizes the shared Gaussian exponent -- a genuine application of the Rayleigh-Ritz variational theorem: minimizing over a real parameter can only lower (never raise) the computed energy toward the true ground state.
H2+ in a minimal 2-Gaussian basis: the variational principle at work

Walter Heitler and Fritz London's 1927 quantum-mechanical treatment of H2 -- the paper usually credited with founding quantum chemistry as a field -- showed for the first time why two hydrogen atoms bind: the symmetric (in-phase) combination of their two atomic orbitals builds up electron density in the region between the nuclei, lowering the energy below that of the separated atoms, while the antisymmetric (out-of-phase) combination depletes density there and raises the energy instead. Their original calculation used two-electron integrals this package does not implement (chemistrykit.quantum.utils.basis_sets stops at the one-electron integrals H2PlusVariational needs for H2+), but the same qualitative physics -- constructive vs. destructive interference of atomic orbitals along the bond axis -- is exactly what H2+'s own bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals show, using the genuine LCAO coefficients solve computes, not an assumed equal-weight combination.
Heitler-London's insight: bonding vs. antibonding electron density

chemistrykit.quantum.systems.rigid_rotor: Builds an HCl-like RigidRotor from its atomic masses and bond length (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.rigid_rotor.RigidRotor.from_diatomic), plots its energy-level diagram (each level's height showing its (2J+1)-fold degeneracy), and shows that the J\to J+1 microwave absorption lines are evenly spaced by 2B.

chemistrykit.spectro.utils.lineshapes.ga: Compares the three standard spectral lineshapes at matched FWHM: a Lorentzian (the shape a classically radiating damped oscillator, or a finite-lifetime quantum transition, produces -- "homogeneous" broadening, identical for every molecule in the sample), a Gaussian (the shape a Maxwell-Boltzmann spread of line-of-sight velocities produces via the Doppler effect -- "inhomogeneous" broadening, different molecules contributing different, momentarily Doppler-shifted, sub-lines), and their convolution, the Voigt profile, which is what a real spectrum typically shows once both mechanisms contribute together. The Lorentzian has visibly heavier tails than the Gaussian at the same FWHM -- the qualitative signature used to diagnose which mechanism dominates a real measured line.
Gaussian, Lorentzian, and Voigt lineshapes: two broadening mechanisms and their convolution
chemistrykit.spectro.utils.lineshapes.lo: Compares the three standard spectral lineshapes at matched FWHM: a Lorentzian (the shape a classically radiating damped oscillator, or a finite-lifetime quantum transition, produces -- "homogeneous" broadening, identical for every molecule in the sample), a Gaussian (the shape a Maxwell-Boltzmann spread of line-of-sight velocities produces via the Doppler effect -- "inhomogeneous" broadening, different molecules contributing different, momentarily Doppler-shifted, sub-lines), and their convolution, the Voigt profile, which is what a real spectrum typically shows once both mechanisms contribute together. The Lorentzian has visibly heavier tails than the Gaussian at the same FWHM -- the qualitative signature used to diagnose which mechanism dominates a real measured line.
Gaussian, Lorentzian, and Voigt lineshapes: two broadening mechanisms and their convolution

chemistrykit.spectro.visualizers.spectro: Absorbance is exactly linear in concentration by the ideal Beer-Lambert law. A small amount of instrumental stray light (light that reaches the detector without having passed through the fully absorbing sample path) causes the apparent absorbance to fall increasingly below the true value as concentration -- and hence true absorbance -- increases, the classic "rolling over" deviation seen in real UV-Vis instruments.
Beer-Lambert absorbance, and its deviation from linearity at high concentration

Builds a vibronic progression from the Huang-Rhys displacement parameter, verifies the Franck-Condon factors' normalization (they must sum to 1 -- the required correctness check for any Franck-Condon calculation), and shows how a larger excited-state displacement shifts the most-intense vibronic peak to higher v'.
Franck-Condon vibronic progressions in a UV-Vis absorption band

Simulates ethanol's classic -CH3 triplet and -CH2- quartet (each proton set split only by its 3-bond neighbor, the textbook first-order pattern), then a genuine doublet of triplets from two chemically distinct coupling partners with different J values.
